J.
 Langan,
 R.D.
 Seidler
 / Behavioural
 Brain
 Research
 225 (2011) 160–
 168
167
Spatial
 working
 memory
 performance
 (card
 rotation,
 back-
ward
 Corsi
 blocks)
 was
 related
 to
 better
 motor
 transfer
 for
the
 young
 adults.
 These
 results
 parallel
 our
 previous
 ﬁnding
 of
SWM
 contributions
 to
 visuomotor
 adaptation
 in
 young
 adults
[12]
 and
 other
 studies
 demonstrating
 cognitive
 contributions
 to
early
 sensorimotor
 adaptation
 [13–15]. Older
 adults
 demonstrated
correlations
 between
 spatial
 working
 memory
 and
 performance
at
 motor
 transfer
 but
 not
 for
 motor
 learning.
 This
 is
 consis-
tent
 with
 our
 previous
 report
 of
 a
 lack
 of
 correlation
 between
working
 memory
 performance
 and
 visuomotor
 adaptation
 in
older
 adults
 [16],
 suggesting
 that
 a
 failure
 to
 engage
 SWM
 may
be
 related
 to
 motor
 learning
 deﬁcits.
 Surprisingly,
 older
 adults
with
 better
 spatial
 working
 memory
 performance
 demonstrated
longer
 RTs
 at
 motor
 transfer.
 Additionally,
 longer
 reaction
 times
were
 not
 correlated
 with
 better
 transfer
 performance.
 These
results
 underscore
 the
 differential
 impact
 of
 cognitive
 contri-
butions
 to
 motor
 learning
 and
 transfer
 in
 young
 versus
 older
adults.
To
 better
 understand
 whether
 and
 how
 spatial
 working
 memory
contributes
 to
 motor
 learning
 and
 transfer
 we
 used
 a
 mask
 based
on
 brain
 activation
 associated
 with
 SWM
 task
 performance
 to
 iden-
tify
 brain
 regions
 exhibiting
 overlapping
 activation
 during
 both
the
 SWM
 task
 and
 the
 visuomotor
 adaptation
 task.
 In
 our
 recent
work,
 we
 found
 activation
 in
 early
 learning
 that
 overlapped
 with
that
 associated
 with
 SWM
 for
 young
 adults
 [12].
 This
 pattern
 is
similar
 to
 other
 studies
 of
 visuomotor
 transformations
 [27,28]. In
contrast,
 we
 found
 that
 a
 failure
 to
 engage
 SWM
 networks
 during
visuomotor
 adaptation
 by
 older
 adults
 was
 associated
 with
 learning
deﬁcits
 [16].
 Similarly,
 in
 the
 current
 study,
 we
 found
 that
 young
adults
 recruited
 many
 of
 the
 same
 brain
 regions
 for
 SWM
 as
 they
do
 for
 initial
 learning
 of
 the
 visuomotor
 adaptation
 task,
 includ-
ing
 the
 bilateral
 superior
 and
 inferior
 parietal
 lobules
 and
 inferior
frontal
 gyri.
 At
 motor
 transfer,
 overlapping
 activation
 reduced
 and
was
 limited
 to
 the
 right
 inferior
 frontal
 and
 inferior
 parietal
 gyri.
These
 data
 suggest
 that
 working
 memory
 processes
 are
 engaged
to
 a
 reduced
 extent
 for
 motor
 transfer
 versus
 learning.
 In
 the
 cur-
rent
 study,
 neural
 overlap
 between
 the
 SWM
 task
 and
 visuomotor
adaptation
 for
 the
 older
 adults
 was
 limited
 to
 the
 left
 superior
and
 inferior
 parietal
 lobules,
 with
 minimal
 change
 between
 initial
motor
 learning
 and
 transfer.
Young
 adults
 engaged
 an
 extensive
 overlapping
 network
 of
brain
 regions
 for
 motor
 learning
 and,
 to
 a
 reduced
 extent,
 for
 motor
transfer
 including
 prefrontal,
 premotor,
 occipital,
 and
 parietal
 cor-
tices.
 In
 contrast,
 overlapping
 activation
 for
 older
 adults
 was
 limited
to
 the
 parietal
 cortex.
 The
 superior
 parietal
 lobule
 plays
 a
 role
in
 working
 memory,
 speciﬁcally
 in
 the
 ability
 to
 manipulate
 and
rearrange
 information
 [29].
 The
 lateral
 prefrontal
 cortex
 is
 thought
to
 support
 mechanisms
 of
 attention,
 interference
 resolution,
 and
retrieval
 mechanisms
 in
 working
 memory
 [30]. It
 is
 typical
 that
older
 adults
 exhibit
 under-recruitment
 of
 the
 lateral
 prefrontal
 cor-
tex
 in
 cognitive
 tasks
 (cf.
 [31]).
 The
 lack
 of
 prefrontal
 activation
 in
older
 adults
 here
 may
 indicate
 that
 they
 are
 not
 engaging
 the
 appro-
priate
 attentional
 and
 strategic
 mechanisms
 required
 for
 motor
learning.
Direct
 comparisons
 of
 young
 and
 older
 adults’
 brain
 activation
patterns
 at
 initial
 motor
 learning
 revealed
 that
 young
 adults
 more
strongly
 engaged
 the
 left
 postcentral
 gyrus,
 right
 superior
 frontal
gyrus
 and
 right
 middle
 occipital
 lobule
 compared
 to
 older
 adults,
whereas
 the
 older
 adults
 more
 strongly
 recruited
 the
 right
 post-
central
 gyrus
 and
 paracentral
 lobule.
 Finding
 greater
 activation
 in
the
 right
 sensorimotor
 cortex
 for
 older
 adults
 is
 compatible
 with
what
 has
 been
 reported
 for
 other
 motor
 tasks
 ([32–34]; for
 a
 recent
review
 see
 ref.
 [35]).
 At
 motor
 transfer
 the
 young
 adults
 demon-
strated
 greater
 activation
 in
 the
 basal
 ganglia
 and
 cingulate
 gyrus
compared
 to
 older
 adults.
 Both
 of
 these
 regions
 have
 been
 reported
to
 contribute
 to
 visuomotor
 adaptation
 [36],
 and
 to
 play
 a
 role
 in
 detection
 and
 correction
 processes
 [37,38]. The
 present
 ﬁnd-
ings
 suggest
 that
 young
 adults
 may
 be
 better
 able
 to
 engage
 these
processes
 to
 modulate
 performance
 at
 transfer
 of
 learning.
Both
 age
 groups
 exhibited
 transfer
 under
 the
 two
 rotation
 pre-
sentation
 orders,
 with
 the
 older
 adults
 exhibiting
 more
 transfer
than
 the
 young
 to
 the
 45◦condition
 and
 the
 young
 exhibiting
 more
than
 the
 old
 to
 the
 30◦condition.
 We have
 previously
 shown
 that
transfer
 is
 greater
 for
 young
 adults
 when
 the
 ﬁnal
 rotation
 reﬂects
an
 addition
 of
 previously
 experienced
 rotation
 magnitudes
 (i.e.,
30◦, 15◦, 45◦) than
 when
 it
 requires
 a
 subtraction
 (i.e.,
 45◦, 15◦, 30◦
error
[39]).
 This
 is
 consistent
 with
 the
 notion
 that
 adaptation
 occurs
 as
 a
gradual
 process
 starting
 with
 small
 angles
 of
 rotation
 and
 proceed-
ing
 up
 to
 the
 desired
 rotation
 angle
 [40,41]. The
 current
 ﬁndings
suggest
 that
 contrasting
 transfer
 mechanisms
 for
 additive
 versus
subtractive
 processes
 are
 compounded
 by
 age.
5.
 Conclusions
In conclusion,
 we found
 that
 both
 age
 groups
 exhibited
 positive
motor
 transfer
 for
 at
 least
 some
 variables.
 Young
 adults
 exhib-
ited
 both
 neural
 and
 behavioral
 overlap
 between
 SWM
 and
 motor
learning
 and
 transfer
 performance.
 For
 older
 adults,
 neural
 over-
lap
 between
 SWM
 and
 motor
 learning
 and
 transfer
 was
 restricted
to
 the
 parietal
 cortex
 and
 showed
 minimal
 changes
 from
 motor
learning
 to
 transfer.
Role
 of
 the
 funding
 source
The
 sponsors
 played
 no
 role
 in
 study
 design;
 in
 the
 collection,
analysis,
 and
 interpretation
 of
 data,
 in
 the
 writing
 of
 the
 report;
 nor
in
 the
 decision
 to
 submit
 the
 paper
 for
 publication.
